blindSummary: This is a low-hazard destination for transgender visitors. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016; the constitution guarantees equal protection; and the country is a small, tourism-dependent island nation with extremely low violent crime and long exposure to international visitors. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-specific infrastructure, but also no documented pattern of anti-trans violence or police hostility.
blindOutOfScope: The absence of legal gender recognition is resident-facing; evidence is thin given the very small population.
blindSourceSummaries: A university's gender-justice resource page on this country: the constitution guarantees fundamental rights - one provision prohibits torture, another affirms equal protection and prohibits discrimination including on the basis of sex; same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016.

LGBT news outlet (May 2016): this country repealed a historic penal-code provision (up to 14 years for male same-sex 'unnatural offences') via a 2016 penal-code amendment - the president had highlighted the need to abolish criminalising provisions; tourism (~20% of GDP) had made the destination a 'no-go' area for LGBT tourism.

A university's online history sourcebook: an ancient legal code (c. 1075 BCE) - a background reference on the history of laws concerning same-sex acts (a general historical source, not about this country).
An LGBT travel-guide website's page on this country: a country guide covering the legal situation and travel considerations for prospective visitors.
An encyclopedia-derived summary site: LGBT rights in this country - pre-repeal snapshot noting male 'carnal knowledge against the order of nature' was illegal while female same-sex acts were legal.

A global decriminalisation-news site (Sept 2024): reporting that this country has moved from having anti-gay laws to protecting its LGBTQ citizens - a new penal-code amendment bill (passed 18-8) increases sentences for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability; per an international legal-aid trust, it became the second country in its region, after a regional peer, to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation.
blindLocalsOnly: No legal gender recognition - a resident-facing gap.
blindTangential: The 2016 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
